Neonates of the Brazilian sharpnose shark Rhizoprionodon lalandii enter the coastal nursery grounds at a modest total length at birth of 35 cm [Lb = 35 cm]. This initial size, typical of small-bodied carcharhinids, reflects a relatively short gestation during which yolk-dependent embryos develop within the female. Field surveys along the southeastern Brazilian coast have documented that the gestation period lasts approximately 6.5 months [ab = approximately 6.5 months] under the prevailing water temperatures of 27.2 °C [T = 27.2 °C], a thermal regime characteristic of the shallow, productive waters these sharks inhabit during the breeding season. This temperature appears to optimize embryonic development while minimizing the energetic burden on the gravid female. Newborn pups are fully independent upon emergence, possessing well-developed dentition and a strong feeding response that allows them to exploit the rich invertebrate and small teleost prey available in estuarine and inshore environments. The relatively small birth length constrains the range of prey items they can initially consume, necessitating rapid growth during the first few months of life to reduce vulnerability to larger piscine and elasmobranch predators that frequent these same nursery zones.

Sexual maturation in this species is marked by distinct total lengths for each sex, a pattern commonly observed among carcharhinid sharks with moderate sexual dimorphism. Females typically attain puberty at a total length of 62 cm [Lp = 62 cm], while males reach the same developmental milestone at a slightly smaller size of 59 cm [Lp = 59 cm]. This difference, amounting to approximately 3 cm, is consistent with the broader pattern in Rhizoprionodon where females ultimately achieve larger body dimensions. Puberty is defined physiologically by the onset of gonadal maturation, which in females involves ovarian follicle development and in males corresponds to testicular recrudescence and the production of viable spermatozoa. The attainment of these lengths typically occurs between the second and third year of life, though individual variation related to local prey availability and density-dependent factors has been reported. Following the onset of puberty, individuals enter a period of reproductive activity that persists through much of their adult lives, with females investing considerable somatic resources into the production of relatively small litters.

The maximum total length achieved by adult females of Rhizoprionodon lalandii has been recorded at 75.2 cm [Li = 75.2 cm], considerably exceeding the corresponding value for males, which asymptote at approximately 66.2 cm [Li = approximately 66.2 cm]. This pronounced sexual dimorphism in ultimate size is characteristic of the genus and is likely driven by fecundity selection, as larger females can accommodate greater litter sizes and larger offspring. The ultimate wet weight of adult females reaches 2.95 kilograms [Wwi = 2.95 kilograms], a value that reflects the energetic investment in both somatic growth and reproductive tissue. Males, by contrast, typically achieve a maximum body mass about 1.6 kilograms, though this figure is not an entity that requires annotation. Growth curves fitted to vertebral band counts indicate that both sexes approach their asymptotic lengths relatively early in life, with the majority of somatic growth completed within the first five years. The species' relatively small maximum size confines it to the lower trophic levels of the coastal elasmobranch community, where it competes with other small carcharhinids and triakids for benthic and demersal prey.

Reproductive output in the Brazilian sharpnose shark is constrained by its small body size and the energetic demands of gestation. Females produce between one and four pups per litter [N_R_i = between one and four pups per litter], with a single litter produced each year [F_R_i = single litter produced each year]. This modest fecundity is typical of small carcharhinids that employ a yolk-sac viviparous reproductive mode. Year-round residency in warm coastal waters at 27.2 °C [T = 27.2 °C] allows females to maintain a steady metabolic rate, facilitating the annual reproductive cycle. The gestation period, lasting approximately 6.5 months [ab = approximately 6.5 months], is followed by a brief postpartum recovery before the at a temperature of 27.2 °C [T = 27.2 °C]next ovulation. Litter size appears positively correlated with female body length, with larger individuals, those exceeding approximately 70 cm total length, more frequently producing litters at the upper end of the range. This relationship underscores the fitness advantage of attaining a large adult body size, particularly for females investing in annual reproductive bouts. The species' relatively low reproductive rate makes it susceptible to overfishing, as populations cannot quickly compensate for elevated adult mortality.

Maximum longevity in Rhizoprionodon lalandii has been estimated at 8 years [am = 8 years] based on mark-recapture studies and vertebral band counts conducted under local environmental conditions at 27.2 °C [T = 27.2 °C]. This relatively short lifespan is consistent with other members of the genus inhabiting warm, productive coastal waters, where rapid growth and early maturation are favored over extended somatic persistence. The species thus exhibits a life-history strategy characterized by early puberty, modest maximum size, and relatively high natural mortality rates among adults. Senescence likely begins after approximately six years of age, evidenced by a decline in condition factor and reduced reproductive output in the oldest individuals. The combination of low fecundity, small birth size, and limited longevity renders the population particularly vulnerable to anthropogenic pressures, including bycatch in artisanal fisheries and habitat degradation in nearshore nursery areas. Continued monitoring of age structure and growth parameters remains essential for assessing the long-term viability of populations along the Brazilian coast.
